rationale: Mixed-methods empirical study investigating menstrual experiences, sociocultural taboos, and school absenteeism among girls and adolescents in rural schools of the Colombian Pacific. Although poor access to school restrooms and water is noted among the challenges of menstruation and public officials (including from the Vice-ministry of Water and Sanitation) were interviewed regarding policy invisibility of menstrual inequality, the study examines sociocultural constructs around menstruation rather than a legal or administrative rule-type mechanism governing household or community water/sanitation service access (E03).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, the record is excluded (E03) because it examines sociocultural constructs, stigma, and menstrual health challenges in rural schools rather than any legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, enforcement, discretion, or utility-structure rule governing water or sanitation access. Under the literal broad Criterion 2 wording covering any institutional or governance factor, it would be marked 'unsure' because interviews included institutional officers from the Vice-ministry of Water and Sanitation and municipal secretariats alongside findings on poor access to restrooms and water.

evidence_quotes.quote: Objective To understand the challenges and experiences related to menstruation in girls and adolescents from rural communities of the Colombian Pacific.

This study showed that insufficient information at the time of menarche, pain, poor access to restrooms, water and absorbent materials, as well as existing prejudices, cause menstruation to be experienced with pain and concealment.
Inequality in girls and adolescents, derived from constructs around menstruation, goes unnoticed by schools, families, entities and officers in charge of public policy management.
